kurz: How the Traditional IRA and the Roth IRA are taxed, who may deduct or contribute in 2026, when money can come out and how to choose between the two.

bloecke.md:
An individual retirement account (IRA) is not a financial product but a tax wrapper. You open it at a bank, a brokerage firm or an insurer and choose the investments inside it, from savings deposits to index funds. There are two main versions with opposite tax treatment. With a **Traditional IRA**, contributions may be deductible today and every withdrawal is taxed as ordinary income. With a **Roth IRA**, contributions come from taxed income and qualified withdrawals, including all growth, are tax-free.

The federal government pays no allowances into an IRA. Its support works entirely through the tax code, so its value grows with your marginal tax rate. For savers with low incomes who pay little or no income tax, the deduction is worth little; for them, the Saver's Credit described in the lesson "Beyond the IRA and 401(k)" matters more. Which version is better depends on your tax rate today compared with your tax rate when you withdraw the money.

## Contribution limits in 2026

In 2026, you can contribute up to $7,500 to all your IRAs together, Traditional and Roth combined. From age 50, a catch-up contribution of $1,100 is added, for $8,600 in total. The catch-up amount has been indexed to inflation since 2024. You need taxable compensation, such as wages or self-employment income, at least equal to your contribution. Investment income and Social Security benefits do not count. A married couple filing jointly can also fund an IRA for a spouse without earnings, as long as their combined compensation covers both contributions (spousal IRA).

Contributions for 2026 can be made until the tax filing deadline in April 2027, without extensions. There is no longer an upper age limit for Traditional IRA contributions.

bloecke.erklaerung: If neither you nor your spouse is covered by a retirement plan at work, your Traditional IRA contribution is fully deductible at any income. If you are covered, the deduction phases out over an income range based on your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). Within the range, the formula gives the deductible part; above it, contributions are allowed but not deductible. From age 50, use $8,600 instead of $7,500.

bloecke.beispiel: A single person covered by a 401(k) with a MAGI of $85,000 may deduct $7,500 × (91,000 − 85,000) / 10,000 = $4,500. At $89,500, the result is $1,125, rounded up to $1,130.

bloecke.md: Contributions that are not deductible are still allowed. They create basis, money that has already been taxed and is not taxed again on withdrawal. You report it on Form 8606 each year you make a nondeductible contribution. Without this form, you risk paying tax twice on the same money decades later. A Roth IRA is usually the better home for after-tax money, as long as your income permits it.

bloecke.md:
## The Roth IRA

Roth contributions are never deductible, but they buy three advantages. First, qualified withdrawals are completely tax-free, including decades of growth. A withdrawal is qualified if your first Roth IRA contribution was made for a tax year at least five years earlier and you are 59½ or older, disabled, or using up to $10,000 for a first home; heirs also qualify after the five years. Second, you can withdraw your own contributions at any time, without tax or penalty, because withdrawals count as coming from contributions first. Third, a Roth IRA has no required minimum distributions during the owner's lifetime.

The right to contribute directly phases out at higher incomes, from $153,000 to $168,000 for single filers in 2026. Within the range, the same type of formula applies as for the deduction, with a range of $15,000. A single person with a MAGI of $160,000 may contribute $7,500 × 8,000 / 15,000 = $4,000. People above the limit use the backdoor route described in the lesson "Beyond the IRA and 401(k)".

bloecke.md: The comparison assumes that the Traditional saver invests the full pre-tax amount. In practice, the limit is the same $7,500 for both versions. A Roth contribution of $7,500 holds $7,500 of after-tax money, while a Traditional contribution of $7,500 still carries the future tax bill. Savers who already contribute the maximum can therefore shelter more with a Roth. Holding money in both versions creates tax diversification: in retirement, you can choose each year which account to draw from and steer your taxable income.

- **Excess contributions:** amounts above the limit, or above your compensation, cost an excise tax of 6% for every year they stay in the account. Withdraw the excess and its earnings before the filing deadline.
- **Indirect rollovers:** if you take money out of an IRA and redeposit it yourself, you have 60 days and may do this only once in twelve months for all your IRAs. Direct transfers between institutions have no such limit.
- **Ignoring Roth income limits:** if your income turns out to be too high after you have contributed, the contribution is an excess contribution. You can recharacterize it as a Traditional contribution before the filing deadline.

## Withdrawals and required minimum distributions

Withdrawals from a Traditional IRA before age 59½ are taxed as ordinary income and, in addition, generally cost 10% (26 U.S.C. § 72(t)). The main exceptions for IRAs are a first home (up to $10,000 over your lifetime), qualified higher education costs, unreimbursed medical costs above 7.5% of adjusted gross income, health insurance premiums while unemployed, disability, a birth or adoption (up to $5,000), one emergency withdrawal of up to $1,000 a year and a series of substantially equal periodic payments. The rule of 55, which allows penalty-free withdrawals after leaving a job, applies to employer plans but not to IRAs.

From age 73, Traditional IRAs require minimum distributions each year; for people born in 1960 or later, from age 75. The first distribution can be postponed to 1 April of the following year, but then two fall into the same year. If you miss one, the penalty is 25% of the amount not withdrawn, or 10% if corrected in time. From age 70½, you can transfer IRA money directly to charity as a qualified charitable distribution, which counts towards the required distribution and is not taxed.

bloecke.md:
## Costs inside the IRA

The tax treatment says nothing about costs. An IRA at a large brokerage firm usually has no account fee, and broad index funds and ETFs with a [[Total expense ratio (TER)|total expense ratio]] well below 0.1% a year are widely available. Expensive solutions come from other sources: actively managed funds with sales charges, advisory fees charged as a percentage of assets every year, and annuities held inside an IRA. An annuity offers tax deferral, which the IRA already provides, so inside an IRA you pay for a feature you have twice. Ask for the total annual cost in dollars before you sign anything.

Whether a Traditional or a Roth IRA comes out ahead depends on the tax rate today compared with the tax rate on withdrawal, and that second rate is unknown when you contribute. If you are in the 10% or 12% bracket today, Roth is usually hard to beat. In the 32% bracket and above, the Traditional deduction usually wins. In between, a mix of both is a reasonable hedge.

bloecke.md:
In federal bankruptcy, Traditional and Roth IRAs are protected up to an inflation-indexed cap of more than $1.5 million; money rolled over from employer plans is protected without a cap (11 U.S.C. § 522(n)). Outside bankruptcy, protection depends on state law.

Since the SECURE Act of 2019, most beneficiaries other than a spouse must empty an inherited IRA by the end of the tenth year after the owner's death. If the owner had already begun required distributions, annual distributions are also due in years one to nine. A surviving spouse can treat the IRA as his or her own. An inherited Roth IRA remains tax-free, while every dollar from an inherited Traditional IRA is taxable income for the heir, often in the heir's peak earning years.

- Contribute early in the year if you can; the deadline is the tax filing deadline in April 2027, but every month invested counts.
- Check whether you or your spouse are covered by a workplace plan; Box 13 of the W-2 shows it.
- Estimate your MAGI before contributing to a Roth IRA. If you end up above the limit, recharacterize before the deadline.
- File Form 8606 for every nondeductible contribution and keep copies permanently.
- Choose low-cost index funds inside the IRA. The wrapper is only as good as what it holds.
- Name beneficiaries on the account and review them after marriage, divorce or a death.

mitnehmen: An IRA is a tax wrapper, not a product; the Traditional IRA gives a deduction today and taxes withdrawals, the Roth IRA taxes contributions and frees qualified withdrawals from tax.

In 2026, up to $7,500 can go into all IRAs together, plus $1,100 from age 50; the Traditional deduction phases out if you are covered at work, and direct Roth contributions phase out from $153,000 for single filers.
With equal tax rates today and in retirement, both versions end with the same amount; the version taxed at the lower of the two rates wins.

begriffe.text: Individual retirement account whose contributions are deductible within income limits and whose withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income. Withdrawals before 59½ generally cost an additional 10% tax; required minimum distributions start at 73 or 75.

Individual retirement account funded with after-tax money. Qualified withdrawals after five years and from 59½ are tax-free, contributions can be withdrawn at any time, and there are no required distributions for the owner. Direct contributions are limited by income.
Adjusted gross income with certain deductions and exclusions added back. It determines whether you may deduct Traditional IRA contributions and contribute directly to a Roth IRA.

Annual minimum withdrawal from pre-tax retirement accounts, starting at 73 for those born from 1951 to 1959 and at 75 for those born in 1960 or later. A missed distribution costs 25% of the shortfall, or 10% if corrected in time.
The part of a Traditional IRA that comes from nondeductible contributions and has therefore already been taxed. It is tracked on Form 8606 and is not taxed again on withdrawal.
IRA for a spouse with little or no compensation, funded on the basis of the other spouse's compensation. It requires joint filing; combined compensation must cover both contributions.
